claim: Averaging two guesses from one person beats either guess alone on factual percentage and quantity questions, but the gain is small (about 8 percent lower squared error: 541 vs 589 in the large replication; 95% CI of error cut 2.5-10.4 percent immediate in the original).
agent_test: Same-model pairs: compare mean of two numeric answers vs one, at equal tokens against two plain single-answer samples.
audit_note: Numbers verified in Vul and Pashler and Steegen et al.; minor: the verified studies used percentage questions only (CIA Factbook), so 'and quantity' is slightly wider than shown.

claim: Averaging two guesses from the same person is worth only about 1.1 to 1.3 independent people (Vul and Pashler: lambda 0.11 immediate, 0.32 delayed, i.e. a second guess is worth 11-32% of a second person's guess; 1.04-1.07 in a replication by Hourihan and Benjamin); even an ensemble of five different thinking styles reaches only about 1.5 people (Fujisaki et al. 2025); asking another person beat re-asking oneself in all six conditions of Gomilsek et al. 2024.
agent_test: Measure lambda for the agent: error of the mean of k same-model samples vs the mean of k samples from different prompts or models; expect lambda near 0 to 0.3.
audit_note: Numbers match, but 1.1-1.5 is the equivalent number of people for the whole averaged set (lambda 0.11/0.32 is the second guess's worth), and the 'field data say barely better than two different people' clause is not in any opened source (Gomilsek only shows asking someone else wins in all 6 conditions, +8.3 points).
claim_before_audit: A second guess from the same person is worth only about 1.1 to 1.5 independent people, far below a second person (lambda 0.11 immediate, 0.32 delayed; 1.04-1.07 in a replication; about 1.5 even for a five-style ensemble; field data say barely better than two different people).

claim: More repeated plain estimates from one person do not keep helping: error is flat from 1 to 5 own estimates.
agent_test: Plot accuracy vs number of plain samples for numeric tasks and check whether it flattens after 2 to 3. Only the Fujisaki lab (two papers) and an unopened original support the human result.

claim: Whether a delay between guesses helps is contested: the original and field data say yes; the replication found it only against guess 2, not guess 1 (gain 50 vs 48, BF about 12.9 for no difference); a 2026 perceptual study found no delay gain.
agent_test: Test fresh-context vs same-context second samples (the agent analogue of a delay: memory of guess 1 removed). Compare error of the mean at equal tokens.

claim: Expertise or training that narrows the answer distribution removes the inner-crowd gain while the outer-crowd gain stays (numerosity: inner variance term a=0.05 untrained vs 0.005 trained, BF10 0.02).
agent_test: Skip resampling when repeated samples already agree. Measure how often spread is zero on our tasks.

claim: Strong LLMs often repeat the same answer in every sample, leaving no variance to average (78 of 108 GPT-4/4o experiments had near-zero SD over 30 runs at T=0.8), and open-ended samples are very similar (79 percent of cases mean similarity above 0.8). Gap search adds: Qwen3-1.7B at T=1.5 on MMLU-Pro had 32.7 percent near-unanimous questions (top answer in 12 of 16 votes or more); two calls of Qwen2.5-7B at T=0.2 disagreed on about 0.6 percent of binary items; Gemini-2.5-Pro on MATH-500 was already at 98 percent single-pass so 15 samples added 1.6 points.
agent_test: Measure per-item answer entropy over 5 samples at T=0.7-1.0 on our benchmarks; report the share of items with zero spread.
audit_note: Minor: Lou and Sun's 78/108 is numeric answers in anchoring experiments; 32.7% is the share with top letter in >=12 of 16 votes (3,933 of 12,032).

claim: Inner-crowd gain is larger on hard items and weaker models and small near ceiling or on easy items (a disagreeing second guess helps hard items, hurts easy ones; self-consistency +17.9 at PaLM GSM8K 56.5 but +1.8 at AddSub 91.9; Agent Forest relative gain 200 percent MATH vs 16 percent GSM8K GPT-3.5).
agent_test: Route resampling by a first-pass difficulty signal (disagreement between 2 samples) and compare with uniform resampling at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: the Agent Forest 200% (MATH) is Llama2-13B while the 16% (GSM8K) is GPT-3.5, so the pair confounds model and task; the paper itself reports MATH 34%-200% vs GSM8K 16%-69% and Llama2-13B 28%-200% vs GPT-3.5 8%-16%.

claim: Dialectical bootstrapping (assume the first guess is wrong, give reasons, estimate again) is contested, leaning not supported as better than a plain second guess: the original reported a larger gain, but White and Antonakis (source opened) show that gain comes from a score tied to how often the second guess equals the first (0.7 vs 20.2 percent identical); with untied scores both groups gain the same (d=0.38 vs 0.39, interaction F(1,99)=0.00, p=.98). A 2026 group reanalysis (abstract only) says dialectical bootstrapping worsened mean crowd accuracy. Earlier: a control-condition gain of d=0.12 with CI including zero; a 2024 test with no strategy difference untrimmed (d=0.007) but a difference when 20 percent trimmed.
agent_test: LLM analogue: forced 'assume wrong' second sample vs plain second sample, combined by code, equal tokens. Prior LLM evidence (Huang) says no gain.

claim: People cannot tell when to average their own guesses: chosen answers are near chance (47-57 percent accuracy; 67 needed to beat always averaging), so always averaging beats choosing.
agent_test: Compare a fixed code rule (always combine) with a model-chosen pick between its own two answers; expect the fixed rule to win.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Taking another perspective or using different thinking styles for the next estimate raises independence and gain over plain repeats (bracketing 35 vs 22 percent; five-style ensemble keeps improving, d=0.59), but the net is still about 1.5 persons and one large experiment found no overall effect. Gap search: a 2026 reanalysis from the same research tradition (abstract only) reports mixed-instruction crowds did not beat the best single instruction at any group size, and a disagreeing-perspective instruction moved answers without improving crowd accuracy on average.
agent_test: Five prompts varying framing vs five temperature samples, same model, equal tokens; vote or average.

claim: Majority vote over many sampled reasoning chains from one LLM gives large gains over greedy chain-of-thought on tasks with discrete answers (PaLM-540B GSM8K 56.5 to 74.4; GPT-3.5 GSM8K 76.7 at 1 sample vs 82.5 / 85.3 / 88.2 at 3 / 6 / 9; Llama2-13B GSM8K 0.35 to 0.59).
agent_test: Already our best-of-N arm; report accuracy per token against the plain model.
audit_note: Huang (GSM8K 76.7 -> 82.5/85.3/88.2) and Li et al. (Llama2-13B 0.35 -> 0.59 in Table, Agent Forest) verified; Wang et al. numbers not opened in the paper itself (PDF download failed).

claim: Asking one LLM to rethink its own answer with no external feedback does not help and often hurts (CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after 5 calls), while equal-budget voting helps.
agent_test: Supports G2. Include a forced self-review arm to confirm it fails on our tasks.
audit_note: Huang numbers verified; Zeng et al. supports the qualitative claim for long-CoT models (sequential self-revision gives limited/oscillating gains, parallel scales better) but is a different setting.

claim: Voting gains plateau near 100 samples while the pool of correct answers keeps growing, so selection is the bottleneck (MATH Llama-3-8B coverage 82.9 to 98.44 percent, vote 40.50 to 41.41 percent).
agent_test: Report coverage (any sample right) vs vote accuracy vs check-picked accuracy at 8, 16, 32 samples.
audit_note: Numbers verified in Large Language Monkeys (plateau near 100 samples, 82.9->98.44 coverage vs 40.50->41.41 vote); the plateau and bottleneck claim rests on that single paper, Wang et al. only say SC saturates quickly within 40 samples.

claim: For LLM probability and numeric forecasting, resampling the same system gives small gains in one study (trimmed mean Brier 0.1676 to 0.1649, about 1.6 percent) and larger ones in another (7 to 35 percent, abstract only); not settled. Gap search: the combiner does not explain the gap, because mean, median, geometric mean and trimmed mean were within 0.0007 Brier of each other at 6 forecasts (.1656, .1651, .1655, .1649), while LLM-as-aggregator (USC) was worse than no ensemble (.1691 vs .1676). The 7 to 35 percent figure (500 draws) could not be opened (SSRN returned 403), so sample count remains a possible explanation.
agent_test: Forecast tasks: average 5 same-model probabilities vs single with a trimmed mean; compare Brier.

claim: Averaging own samples cannot fix shared bias: LLM errors are highly correlated (agreement about 60 percent when both wrong), averaging removes variance not bias, and acquiescence bias persists in LLM crowds. Ariely 2000 is now read first-hand: for judged probabilities, averaging a person's own two estimates left the probability score almost unchanged (.252 to .250) while averaging two people improved it (.234), N=64.
agent_test: Measure what fraction of wrong majority answers are also the modal single-sample answer.
audit_note: Minor: 'averaging removes variance not bias' is the diversity-prediction/Vul-Pashler framing rather than a tested result; Kim et al. 60% is the Helm figure.

claim: Mixing in a different source (another person, or a human crowd forecast) beats a self-update: asking another person was better in all six conditions (mean 8.3 points); a plain machine+human average beat the model's own update after seeing the human median.
agent_test: Combine the model's answer with a code-run check or retrieved evidence by a fixed rule rather than asking the model to revise.
audit_note: Minor: 8.3 is percentage points of how often the other person's estimate gave the better average, not an error reduction.

claim: Varying the approach, not only the sampling noise, can beat same-prompt sampling (DIV-SE GPT-4 graph coloring 97 vs SC-10 23), but other tests find no net gain: mixed prompt sets were worse than plain resampling (PaLM GSM8K 58.9 vs 74.4); prompt-template voting changed accuracy by only +-4 points on average, mixed in sign, across 12 benchmarks even though it lowered sample correlation in 55 of 57 cells; prompt variants failed to beat temperature sampling on AIMO 3; persona prompting reduced accuracy in a 23-model study; and mixing models can drag quality down (Self-MoA beats mixed MoA by 3.8 to 6.6 percent). Likely reading: variation decorrelates but members get weaker, so the net is near zero unless every variant is as strong as the plain prompt.
agent_test: Three arms at equal tokens: temperature-only samples, prompt-diverse samples, mixed-model samples; vote.

claim: Debate between copies of one model beats a single agent but not equal-budget voting: self-consistency matched or beat debate in 93 percent of 980 matched settings (5 open models, 4 tasks), and a 23-model study found debate tied or lost to matched-budget sampling/voting at 1.6x wall-clock and 3.4x tokens. The original debate paper (Du et al.) compared only against a 3-agent majority baseline that was not budget-matched; Huang et al. found debate underperforms self-consistency at equal response counts.
agent_test: Already ruled by G9; keep the equal-token arm as the check.
audit_note: Numbers (93% of 980 settings; 23 models, 1.6x wall-clock, 3.4x tokens) match the abstracts, but the final sentence 'Only the original debate paper lacked this control' is a sweeping universal no source supports (Du et al. did include a 3-agent majority baseline, just not budget-matched); '9-sample' not on the abstract page.
claim_before_audit: Debate between copies of one model beats a single agent but not equal-budget voting: self-consistency matched or beat debate in 93 percent of 980 matched settings (5 open models, 4 tasks), and a 23-model study found debate tied or lost to 9-sample voting at 1.6x wall-clock and 3.4x tokens. Only the original debate paper lacked this control.

claim: Raising sampling temperature up to 1.0 does not significantly change single-sample accuracy, so temperature is a cheap lever for spread.
agent_test: Check accuracy vs temperature (0.3 to 1.0) on our own model.

claim: Listing several answers with probabilities in one call restores diversity lost to alignment (1.6 to 2.1 times diversity in creative writing), but diversity is not accuracy.
agent_test: Open-mode arm: verbalized list vs independent samples, scored by distinct answers and by held-out check.

claim: The inner crowd also appears in perceptual decisions (face matching, AUC gain 5.9 percent after 2 decisions, 7.9 after 3), smaller than between-person aggregation.
agent_test: Boundary note only.

claim: Working-memory span moderates the gain (r=-.16; 1.07 vs 1.04 persons), explained by smaller memory samples overlapping less across guesses.
agent_test: No agent analogue; very weak effect.

claim: Averaging two confidence judgments from one person improves them (d=0.67 to 1.44 over taking the higher one in three datasets), except when accuracy is high.
agent_test: Check whether averaging two verbalized confidences beats one on calibration (abstract only so far).

claim: Same-model votes are worth about 1.3 to 2.9 independent votes, whatever the sample count. Two independent measurements on small open models agree: correctness correlation 0.45 to 0.60 on GSM8K gives a ceiling of 1.7 to 2.2 effective votes, reached by K=8 to 16 (Yu et al. 2026); error correlation 0.35 to 0.77 across five models and four tasks gives a cap of 1/rho (Nguyen et al. 2026). Nine different frontier models gave only about 2.2 effective votes on NLI (Kohli 2026), which suggests, but does not show, that a same-model crowd is no better.
agent_test: On 100 pilot items take 4 samples each; compute pairwise correctness correlation c; effective votes = K/(1+(K-1)c). Report it per task type and per model before choosing k. Not measured for modern frontier or reasoning models.
audit_note: Yu (corr 0.45-0.59/0.60, ceiling 1.71-2.21) and Kohli (n_eff 2.18) check out, but 'so a same-model crowd cannot be better' is an inference from a different-model panel on NLI, not shown by any source; Nguyen rho range 0.35-0.77 and 1/rho cap not seen in abstract (full text pending).
claim_before_audit: Same-model votes are worth about 1.3 to 2.9 independent votes, whatever the sample count. Two independent measurements on small open models agree: correctness correlation 0.45 to 0.60 on GSM8K gives a ceiling of 1.7 to 2.2 effective votes, reached by K=8 to 16 (Yu et al. 2026); error correlation 0.35 to 0.77 across five models and four tasks gives a cap of 1/rho (Nguyen et al. 2026). Nine different frontier models gave only 2.2 effective votes on NLI (Kohli 2026), so a same-model crowd cannot be better.

claim: A cheap pilot predicts how many samples are worth drawing: the two-call disagreement rate caps the gain from 3 or 5 votes (gain is at most half the disagreement rate; Qwen2.5-7B at T=0.2, 0.6 percent disagreement, cap 0.46 points), and a K=4 pilot that estimates the correlation sets the sample budget so that 96 to 103 percent of K=32 accuracy is kept at 25 to 44 percent of the cost.
agent_test: Run 2 samples on a validation slice, compute disagreement and the gain cap, and gate extra sampling on it. Binary or short-answer tasks and small models only; not tested per item.
audit_note: Minor: 0.46 cap uses the Wald upper bound on the 0.6% disagreement rate (point estimate would be ~0.3); 96-103% of K=32 at 25-44% cost holds across model/task rows.

claim: Prompt-template variation lowers sample correlation but changes accuracy little. Mean correlation fell 38 percent (55 of 57 cells; QA -67 percent, math -9 to -29 percent), yet accuracy moved within +-4 points and not in one direction.
agent_test: Measure correlation and accuracy for same-prompt and varied-prompt arms at equal tokens; keep the varied arm only if accuracy rises.

claim: At equal token budgets, independent voting is at least as good as debate, sequential self-revision and one longer chain for 7B-class and distilled reasoning models in three studies, and one study (Qwen3, GPT-OSS, Kimi-K2, 4096-token chains) finds sequential refinement wins 43 of 45 settings. No study tests current frontier reasoning models with a matched budget, and the sequential-win study has internal inconsistencies and tiny test sets.
agent_test: Add an equal-token arm: k independent samples (vote) vs one chain k times longer vs sequential refinement of k steps, on our task types, with a reasoning model.

claim: Samples drawn in a fresh context are less alike than samples that continue from the earlier answer. In code, showing a model its own failed program gave a near-identical retry in 33 to 68 percent of cases vs 2 to 14 percent for a fresh draw, and the fresh draw won at 1.5B and 3B (.749 vs .688 at 1.5B, p=.006) and tied at 7B. In math, re-reading one's own draft gained 0 to 6.7 points at best.
agent_test: Compare similarity and accuracy of k fresh-context samples vs k continued-context samples at equal tokens. Fresh context is the analogue of a delay; no human-style delay effect has been measured for LLMs.

claim: For same-system forecasts the choice among mean, median, geometric mean and trimmed mean does not matter at n=6 (Brier within 0.0007: .1656, .1651, .1655, .1649), and asking a model to combine its own forecasts (USC) was worse than no ensemble (.1691 vs .1676).
agent_test: Combine numeric samples in code with the median; never ask the model to merge them.

claim: Within-person averaging of repeated probability judgments gives almost no gain even when the within-person correlation is about the same as between people (Ariely et al. 2000, N=64: probability score .252 individual, .250 within-person average, .234 between-person average; correlations .66 vs .57).
agent_test: Do not average two verbalized confidences from one model and expect better calibration; test whether two fresh-context confidences help.

claim: Agreement is not accuracy. Nine different frontier models gave all-wrong answers on 5.1 percent of NLI items (under independence, fewer than 1 in 1,000), and unanimous panel answers were right only 90.9 percent of the time. For gpt-4.1 on GPQA, a high-agreement answer (80 percent or more of 50 samples) was wrong 48 percent of the time (CI .40 to .56), and 28 percent of cases were confidently wrong for every runner.
agent_test: Measure the rate of confident wrong majorities on our tasks. Do not use sample agreement alone to skip a check.

claim: Selection, not generation, is the bottleneck for a same-model pool: with a small model on MMLU-Pro (128 samples) majority voting reached 40.7 percent against an oracle of 44.7 percent; a better combiner won back about 38 percent of that gap; and where the correct answer is a minority, majority voting falls as samples are added (20.4 to 6.0 percent from 1 to 16 samples on a selected subset).
agent_test: Report vote accuracy against oracle accuracy at each sample count; use an independent check to pick among distinct answers.
